10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a simplified batch inference job processing a pre-gathered set of inputs, already covered in this topic.

code.content:
def run_batch_inference(inputs, model_weights):
    # already covered as processing a pre-gathered input set in this topic
    predictions = []
    for value in inputs:
        # already covered as batching for hardware efficiency in this topic
        prediction = value * model_weights["scale"] + model_weights["bias"]
        predictions.append({"input": value, "prediction": round(prediction, 3)})
    return predictions

# already covered as a pre-gathered input set in this topic
collected_inputs = [1.2, 3.4, 0.8, 5.1, 2.2]
model_weights = {"scale": 1.5, "bias": 0.1}

print(f"Starting batch inference job on {len(collected_inputs)} already-collected inputs (already covered in this topic)")
results = run_batch_inference(collected_inputs, model_weights)

# already covered as storing results for later use in this topic
print("\nStoring results (already covered in this topic):")
for r in results:
    print(f"  {r}")

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Batch inference processes a large, already-collected set of inputs together, not one request at a time.
Serving answers one live request as it arrives; batch inference flips that into one large processing pass.
A batch job starts from a full set of inputs that are already known before processing begins.
Processing many inputs together uses hardware far more efficiently, reusing the batching idea from Inference.
Because nobody waits live for results, batch inference can prioritize throughput over latency.
Batch jobs typically run on a schedule, processing accumulated data since the previous run.
Results get written somewhere durable, like a database or file, ready for later use.
Batch inference suits large, non-urgent workloads; serving suits requests needing immediate answers.
